subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8! In this unit you will become confident with the world of shapes – the flat, two-dimensional (2D) shapes you can draw on paper and the solid, three-dimensional (3D) shapes you can hold in your hand. You will also study symmetry, the beautiful balance that appears in geometric patterns, in the tiles of a masjid floor, in the petals of a flower, and in the wings of a butterfly. Geometry is one of the oldest branches of mathematics, and it is everywhere around you once you learn to see it.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

outcomes: Identify and describe the parts of a circle – centre, radius, diameter, circumference, chord, arc, sector and tangent – and use the relationship d = 2r.
Classify polygons as regular or irregular and calculate interior and exterior angles.
Recognise and describe the properties of the whole quadrilateral family.
Name 3D solids and count their faces, edges and vertices, and check answers with Euler's formula.
Draw and recognise the nets of common 3D shapes.
Find all the lines of symmetry in a 2D shape.
Determine the order of rotational symmetry of a shape and the angle of rotation.
Sketch and interpret the front view, side view and top view (plan) of a 3D shape built from cubes or a simple solid.

concepts.title: Properties of Circles
concepts.explanation: A circle is the set of all points that are exactly the same distance from a single fixed point. That fixed point is the centre, and the fixed distance is the radius. This one clean idea gives the circle all of its special properties. Circles are everywhere — in wheels, coins, plates, the rim of a well, and the full moon over Mogadishu. Learn these eight parts of a circle carefully, because every circle problem uses them: Tangent: a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point and does not cross into the circle. A tangent is always perpendicular (at a right angle) to the radius drawn to the point where it touches — think of a bicycle wheel touching flat ground, where the ground is the tangent and the spoke to that point is the radius.
concepts.example: Centre: the middle point. Every point on the circle is the same distance from it.

concepts.title: Polygons – Regular and Irregular
concepts.explanation: A polygon is a closed 2D shape made entirely of straight sides. The word comes from Greek and means 'many angles'. A circle is not a polygon because its edge is curved. We name polygons by their number of sides, and this is worth memorising: A polygon is regular when all its sides are equal in length AND all its angles are equal in size. A square and an equilateral triangle are regular. A polygon is irregular when its sides or angles (or both) are not all equal. A rectangle that is not a square is irregular, because its angles are all equal but its sides are not all equal.
concepts.example: The interior angles are the angles inside the polygon at each corner. There is a beautiful rule for their total. Any polygon with n sides has an interior angle sum of (n − 2) × 180°. This works because a polygon can always be split into triangles from one vertex, and each triangle contributes 180°. A quadrilateral splits into 2 triangles, giving (4 − 2) × 180° = 360°. A pentagon splits into 3 triangles, giving (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°. Learn this formula – it is one of the most useful in the whole unit.

concepts.title: The Quadrilateral Family
concepts.explanation:
Quadrilaterals are four-sided polygons, and they form a fascinating family in which each member inherits the properties of the ones above it. Every quadrilateral has four sides, four vertices, and interior angles that add to 360°, and every one can be split into two triangles by a diagonal. Beyond these shared facts, each type adds its own special properties.

Here are the members of the family and what makes each one special:

Trapezium: exactly one pair of parallel sides. An isosceles trapezium has equal legs, equal base angles and one line of symmetry.

Parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal; opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other; rotational symmetry of order 2; no lines of symmetry.

Rectangle: a parallelogram with four right angles; diagonals equal; 2 lines of symmetry; rotational symmetry order 2.

Rhombus: a parallelogram with four equal sides; diagonals cross at right angles and bisect the angles; 2 lines of symmetry; rotational symmetry order 2.

Square: both a rectangle and a rhombus – four equal sides and four right angles; 4 lines of symmetry; rotational symmetry order 4.

Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides; one diagonal bisects the other at right angles; 1 line of symmetry.

Notice the hierarchy: a square is a special rectangle (its sides happen to be equal) and also a special rhombus (its angles happen to be right angles). This is why a square has every property of both. Thinking about the family tree helps you answer tricky true-or-false questions, such as 'Is every square a rectangle?' (Yes – a square meets every rule of a rectangle.) 'Is every rectangle a square?' (No – a rectangle's sides need not all be equal.)
concepts.example: You should also know the area formulas for these shapes, because they turn geometry into useful calculation. For a rectangle, area = length × width. For a square, area = side². For a parallelogram, area = base × height. For a rhombus or a kite, area = (diagonal₁ × diagonal₂) ÷ 2. For a trapezium, area = [(a + b) × height] ÷ 2, where a and b are the two parallel sides. For example, a rhombus with diagonals of 8 cm and 6 cm has area (8 × 6) ÷ 2 = 24 cm².

concepts.title: Three-Dimensional Shapes
concepts.explanation:
Three-dimensional shapes, or solids, have length, width and height. Unlike flat 2D shapes, they take up space and have volume. To describe a solid we use three words. A face is a flat surface. An edge is the line where two faces meet. A vertex (plural vertices) is a corner where edges meet. Counting these three carefully is the key skill of this concept.

Polyhedra are solids with flat faces, straight edges and sharp vertices. Learn these common ones and their counts:

Some solids have curved surfaces and so are not polyhedra. A sphere (like a football) has one curved surface and no edges or vertices. A cylinder (like a tin can) has two flat circular faces and one curved surface. A cone (like an ice-cream cone) has one flat circular base, one curved surface, and one vertex at its point, called the apex.
concepts.example: There is a remarkable rule that connects the parts of any polyhedron, called Euler's formula: V − E + F = 2, where V is the number of vertices, E the number of edges and F the number of faces. Test it on a cube: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. It works! Euler's formula is a brilliant way to check that you have counted correctly. If your numbers do not give 2, you have miscounted somewhere and should count again.

concepts.title: Nets of 3D Shapes
concepts.explanation:
A net is a flat, 2D pattern that folds up to make a 3D solid. Nets are how flat card becomes a box, how a flat sheet of metal becomes a tin, and how you can build a solid shape yourself with scissors and glue. Understanding nets helps you 'see' a 3D shape laid out flat, and it connects 2D and 3D geometry beautifully.

Here are the nets of the most common solids:

Cube: six equal squares joined edge to edge. The most familiar arrangement is a cross or 'T' shape, but there are eleven different nets that all fold into a cube.

Cuboid: six rectangles – three matching pairs – arranged so that opposite faces are equal.

Square-based pyramid: a square in the middle with a triangle attached to each of its four sides.

Triangular prism: two triangles and three rectangles.

Cylinder: two circles (the top and bottom) and one rectangle that wraps around to form the curved surface.

Cone: a circle for the base and a curved 'sector' that wraps up to the apex.
concepts.example: A good test of understanding is to look at a net and predict the solid before folding, or to look at a solid and sketch its net. When Amina makes a small box to hold dates at the market, she draws a cuboid net on card, cuts it out, folds along every edge, and glues the flaps. If she leaves out a face, the box has a hole; if she adds an extra, it will not fold flat. Nets must have exactly the right faces in the right places.

concepts.title: Lines of Symmetry
concepts.explanation:
A line of symmetry (also called a mirror line or axis of symmetry) is a line that divides a shape into two identical halves that are mirror images of each other. If you fold the shape along the line, the two halves match exactly. A quick test is to imagine placing a mirror along the line: if the reflection completes the original shape, it is a true line of symmetry.

Learn the lines of symmetry of the common shapes – these come up constantly:

Infinite – any line through the centre

4 (2 through midpoints, 2 diagonals)

A powerful pattern appears here: a regular polygon with n sides has exactly n lines of symmetry. A regular pentagon has 5, a regular hexagon has 6, a regular octagon has 8. This is a fact worth memorising, because it lets you answer symmetry questions instantly for any regular shape.
concepts.example: Watch out for three common misunderstandings. First, not every shape has a line of symmetry – a scalene triangle and most irregular shapes have none. Second, diagonal lines can be lines of symmetry – a square has two diagonal ones. Third, a line of symmetry does not have to pass through the centre in the obvious way – for an isosceles triangle it runs from the apex down to the middle of the base. Even letters have symmetry: the capital letters A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y have a vertical line of symmetry.

concepts.title: Views of 3D Shapes – Front, Side and Top
concepts.explanation: A single flat drawing cannot show every side of a solid at once, so builders, engineers and designers describe a 3D shape using three separate 2D views: the front view (what you see looking straight at the shape from the front), the side view (what you see looking straight at it from the side, usually the right), and the top view or plan (what you see looking straight down from above). Each view is drawn flat, as if you had closed one eye and traced the outline you can see, ignoring depth. To find each view, imagine the shape sitting on a table in front of you. The front view ignores how deep the shape is; the side view ignores how wide it is; the top view ignores how tall it is. Together, the three views usually give enough information to picture the whole solid, even without seeing it in 3D.
concepts.example: A cuboid made of 1 cm cubes is 4 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 3 cubes tall, sitting with its long edge facing you. The front view is a rectangle 4 squares wide and 3 squares tall (length × height). The side view is a rectangle 2 squares wide and 3 squares tall (width × height). The top view is a rectangle 4 squares wide and 2 squares deep (length × width). For a triangular prism lying on its rectangular face with the triangular ends facing left and right, the front view is a rectangle, the top view is a rectangle, but the side view is a triangle — because looking at it end-on shows the triangular cross-section.

methods.title: Find the radius and circumference of a circle
methods.example: A circular well cover in Garissa has a diameter of 84 cm. What is its radius, and how far is it around the edge (use π ≈ 3.14)?
steps: Divide the diameter by 2 to find the radius.
Multiply the diameter by π (≈ 3.14) to find the circumference: C = πd.
Check that your circumference is a little more than 3 times the diameter.

methods.title: Find each interior angle of a regular polygon
methods.example: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.
steps: Count the sides, n.
Work out the total: (n − 2) × 180°.
Divide the total by n to get each angle.

methods.title: Find the number of sides from an angle
methods.example: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides does it have, and what is its name?
steps: Find the exterior angle: 180° − the interior angle.
Divide 360° by the exterior angle to get n.
Name the polygon from its number of sides.

methods.title: Area of a trapezium
methods.example: A trapezium-shaped garden bed has parallel sides of 10 m and 6 m, and a height of 4 m. Find its area.
steps: Add the two parallel sides first, then multiply by the height before halving.
Check by re-doing the calculation in a different order: 4 × 16 ÷ 2 should still give 32.

methods.title: Euler's formula
methods.example: A triangular prism has 5 faces and 6 vertices. Use Euler's formula to find the number of edges.
steps: Euler's formula is V − E + F = 2.
Put in V = 6 and F = 5: 6 − E + 5 = 2, so 11 − E = 2, which gives E = 9 edges.
This matches the known count for a triangular prism.

methods.title: Lines of symmetry
methods.example: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have, and where do they run?
steps: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry, so a regular pentagon has 5.
Each one runs from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Check by counting the vertices of your regular polygon — they should match the number of lines of symmetry.

workedExamples.title: Radius and diameter
workedExamples.prompt: A circular well cover in Garissa has a diameter of 84 cm. What is its radius, and how far is it around the edge (use π ≈ 3.14)?
workedExamples.solution: Radius = d ÷ 2 = 84 ÷ 2 = 42 cm. Circumference = πd ≈ 3.14 × 84 = 263.76 cm. So the radius is 42 cm and the distance around is about 264 cm.

workedExamples.title: Interior angle of a regular polygon
workedExamples.prompt: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.
workedExamples.solution: Use [(n − 2) × 180°] ÷ n with n = 8. That is [(8 − 2) × 180°] ÷ 8 = (6 × 180°) ÷ 8 = 1080° ÷ 8 = 135°. Each interior angle of a regular octagon is 135°.

workedExamples.title: Find the number of sides
workedExamples.prompt: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides does it have, and what is its name?
workedExamples.solution: The exterior angles sum to 360°, so n = 360° ÷ 30° = 12 sides. A 12-sided polygon is a dodecagon.

workedExamples.title: Area of a trapezium
workedExamples.prompt: A trapezium-shaped garden bed has parallel sides of 10 m and 6 m, and a height of 4 m. Find its area.

workedExamples.title: Euler's formula
workedExamples.prompt: A triangular prism has 5 faces and 6 vertices. Use Euler's formula to find the number of edges.
workedExamples.solution: Euler's formula is V − E + F = 2. Put in V = 6 and F = 5: 6 − E + 5 = 2, so 11 − E = 2, which gives E = 9 edges. This matches the known count for a triangular prism.

workedExamples.title: Lines of symmetry
workedExamples.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have, and where do they run?
workedExamples.solution: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry, so a regular pentagon has 5. Each one runs from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

workedExamples.title: Order of rotational symmetry
workedExamples.prompt: A shape looks identical every 72° as it turns. What is its order of rotational symmetry, and name a shape it could be.
workedExamples.solution: Order = 360° ÷ angle = 360° ÷ 72° = 5. A shape with order 5 could be a regular pentagon.

workedExamples.title: Classifying a quadrilateral
workedExamples.prompt: A quadrilateral has four equal sides, and its diagonals cross at right angles but are not equal in length. What is it — a square or a rhombus? Explain.
workedExamples.solution: Four equal sides point to a rhombus or a square. In a square the diagonals are equal; here they are not equal, so the shape must be a rhombus. (A rhombus has four equal sides but its angles are not right angles, so its diagonals differ in length.)

workedExamples.title: Find the area of
workedExamples.prompt: Find the area of a) a rhombus with diagonals 12 cm and 5 cm b) a trapezium with parallel sides 9 m and 7 m and height 6 m.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: For each solid, give the faces, edges and vertices: a) cuboid b) square-based pyramid c) tetrahedron.
workedExamples.solution: a) Cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. b) Square-based pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices. c) Tetrahedron: 4 faces, 6 edges, 4 vertices. (Check each with Euler’s formula V − E + F = 2.)

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: State the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a rhombus.
workedExamples.solution: A rhombus has 2 lines of symmetry (along each diagonal) and rotational symmetry of order 2 (angle of rotation 180°).

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: A regular polygon has an interior angle of 156°. How many sides does it have?

activities.title: Build a Solid From Its Net
activities.materials: card or thick paper, a ruler, scissors, glue or tape, a pencil.
steps: Draw the net of a cube: six equal squares in a cross shape, each side about 5 cm.
Add a small glue flap to some edges, then cut the whole net out in one piece.
Fold carefully along every edge and glue the flaps to make a closed cube.
Now try a square-based pyramid: one square with a triangle on each side. Build and compare.
As you fold, name each face, edge and vertex. Count them and check your cube with Euler's formula V − E + F = 2.

activities.title: The Fold-and-Cut Symmetry Test
steps: Fold a square of paper in half, then in half again, then along a diagonal.
Cut small shapes out of the folded edges, then open it up.
Look at the pattern: mark every line of symmetry you can find.
Try folding a rectangle instead of a square and see how the number of symmetry lines changes.
This is exactly how the geometric cut-paper patterns seen in many homes are made – symmetry turned into art.

activities.title: The Rotational Symmetry Spinner
activities.materials: card, a pencil, a pin or split pin, a protractor.
steps: Cut out a shape such as a square, an equilateral triangle, and a parallelogram.
Pin each shape through its centre so it can spin, and trace its outline on paper.
Turn the shape slowly and count how many times it fits its own outline in one full turn.
Record the order of rotational symmetry for each shape and the angle of rotation (360° ÷ order).

activities.title: Household Solids Hunt (Family Task)
activities.materials: your home and family, and a notebook.
steps: Walk around your home with a family member (or by yourself if no one is available) and find real 3D solids: a tin (cylinder), a box (cuboid), a ball (sphere), a dice (cube).
For each polyhedron, count the faces, edges and vertices together.
Check every polyhedron with Euler's formula V − E + F = 2.
Discuss why food is often packaged in cuboids (they stack) and drinks in cylinders (they roll and hold liquid well).

activities.title: Design an Islamic-Style Tiling Pattern
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a protractor, coloured pencils.
steps: Choose a regular polygon that tiles: a triangle, a square, or a hexagon.
Carefully draw copies edge to edge so there are no gaps or overlaps.
Colour the pattern to bring out its symmetry, as artists do in mosque decoration.
Mark the lines of symmetry and the centre of rotation in your finished pattern.

activities.title: Polygon Angle Investigation
steps: Draw a triangle, a quadrilateral, and a pentagon of any shape you like.
Measure every interior angle with your protractor and add them up for each shape.
Compare your totals to 180°, 360° and 540°. How close are you?
Explain why any small measuring errors do not change the true rule (n − 2) × 180°.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand faces, edges and vertices best? Which kind of symmetry – line or rotational – did you find easier to spot, and why? What shape or pattern would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher or your AI tutor at your next session.

rules.title: Circle Circumference Formula
rules.text: The distance around a circle, its circumference, is linked to the diameter by the famous constant π (pi), which is approximately 3.14 (or roughly 22/7). The rule is C = πd, and because d = 2r we can also write C = 2πr. For example, a bicycle wheel with radius 35 cm has a circumference of 2 × π × 35 = 70π ≈ 219.9 cm, which is exactly how far the bicycle rolls forward in one full turn of the wheel. You will study π in much more detail in a later unit; for now, just remember that it links a circle's distance around to its distance across.

rules.title: Interior Angle Sum Formula
rules.text: The interior angles are the angles inside the polygon at each corner. There is a beautiful rule for their total. Any polygon with n sides has an interior angle sum of (n − 2) × 180°. This works because a polygon can always be split into triangles from one vertex, and each triangle contributes 180°. A quadrilateral splits into 2 triangles, giving (4 − 2) × 180° = 360°. A pentagon splits into 3 triangles, giving (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°. Learn this formula – it is one of the most useful in the whole unit.

rules.title: Exterior Angle Sum Rule
rules.text: The exterior angle sits on a straight line with the interior angle at a corner, so an interior angle and its exterior angle always add to 180°. There is a wonderfully simple rule: the exterior angles of any polygon always sum to 360°, no matter how many sides it has. So for a regular polygon, each exterior angle is just 360° ÷ n. This gives a quick way to work backwards: if each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 40°, then it has 360° ÷ 40° = 9 sides, so it is a nonagon.

rules.title: Quadrilateral Hierarchy
rules.text: Notice the hierarchy: a square is a special rectangle (its sides happen to be equal) and also a special rhombus (its angles happen to be right angles). This is why a square has every property of both. Thinking about the family tree helps you answer tricky true-or-false questions, such as 'Is every square a rectangle?' (Yes – a square meets every rule of a rectangle.) 'Is every rectangle a square?' (No – a rectangle's sides need not all be equal.)

rules.title: Euler's Formula for Polyhedra
rules.text: There is a remarkable rule that connects the parts of any polyhedron, called Euler's formula: V − E + F = 2, where V is the number of vertices, E the number of edges and F the number of faces. Test it on a cube: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. It works! Euler's formula is a brilliant way to check that you have counted correctly. If your numbers do not give 2, you have miscounted somewhere and should count again.

rules.title: Connect Geometry to Real Life
rules.text: The best way to lock these ideas in is to find them in the real world. Look for the lines of symmetry in a window grille or a decorative pattern in a masjid. Count the faces, edges and vertices of a box of dates or a tin of milk. Notice how the tiles on a floor fit together without gaps. Every time you connect a rule to something real, your understanding grows stronger and the mathematics becomes something you can see, not just something you memorise. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

realProblems.prompt: A decorative panel in a Berbera masjid repeats a regular octagon (interior angle 135°). At each meeting point one octagon and two squares meet. Show whether the angles fit exactly around the point.
realProblems.answer: 135° + 90° + 90° = 315°, which is less than 360°, so this exact combination leaves a 45° gap and does not fit perfectly.

realProblems.prompt: Idris claims a shape with 4 equal sides must be a square. Give a counter-example and explain why he is wrong.
realProblems.answer: A rhombus has 4 equal sides but no right angles, so it is not a square — four equal sides alone do not make a square.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A regular polygon has an interior angle of 156°. How many sides does it have?
A solid has 8 faces and 12 vertices. Use Euler's formula to find the number of edges.
Explain, using interior angles, why regular pentagons cannot tile a flat surface on their own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A regular pentagon's interior angle is 108°; 3 × 108° = 324° (a gap) and 4 × 108° = 432° (an overlap), so they cannot meet exactly at 360°.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A shape has rotational symmetry of order 8. What is its angle of rotation, and how many lines of symmetry would it have if it were a regular polygon?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Angle = 360° ÷ 8 = 45°; a regular 8-sided polygon has 8 lines of symmetry.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Sort these into 'regular' and 'irregular': equilateral triangle, rectangle, square, scalene triangle, regular hexagon. Explain your reasoning for the rectangle.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Regular: equilateral triangle, square, regular hexagon. Irregular: rectangle, scalene triangle. The rectangle is irregular because although its angles are all 90°, its sides are not all equal – regular needs both.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Lines of Symmetry.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A line of symmetry (also called a mirror line or axis of symmetry) is a line that divides a shape into two identical halves that are mirror images of each other. If you fold the shape along the line, the two halves match exactly. A quick test is to imagine placing a mirror along the line: if the reflection completes the original shape, it is a true line of symmetry. Learn the lines of symmetry of the common shapes – these come up constantly:

selfAssessment: I can identify and describe the parts of a circle – centre, radius, diameter, circumference, chord, arc and sector – and use the relationship d = 2r.
I can classify polygons as regular or irregular and calculate interior and exterior angles.
I can recognise and describe the properties of the whole quadrilateral family.
I can name 3D solids and count their faces, edges and vertices, and check answers with Euler's formula.
I can draw and recognise the nets of common 3D shapes.
I can find all the lines of symmetry in a 2D shape.
I can determine the order of rotational symmetry of a shape and the angle of rotation.
